title: T1588.004 — Obtain Capabilities - Digital Certificates
subtitle: Interactive walkthrough of Obtain Capabilities - Digital Certificates with the technique-specific attack path and defender evidence.
aria: Attack simulation, step 1 of 8. Registering a lookalike domain. The attacker registers a domain that copies a company name, for example corp-login-secure.top. The domain is hours old and no certificate exists yet.

steps.title: Registering a lookalike domain
steps.caption: The attacker registers a domain that copies a company name, for example corp-login-secure.top. The domain is hours old and no certificate exists yet.
steps.defender: You see nothing. Registration data is public, but your team is not watching it yet.

steps.title: Requesting a free TLS certificate
steps.caption: The attacker asks a certificate authority for a free domain-validated certificate. The authority only checks that the attacker controls the domain, so it approves within minutes.
steps.defender: First visibility: certificate transparency logs publish the new certificate minutes after issuance. No attack has touched anyone yet.

steps.title: Deploying the phishing page
steps.caption: The attacker uploads a copy of the company login page to the server and turns on HTTPS. The padlock icon now shows, which makes the site look real.
steps.defender: Your users have not visited yet, so your proxy has no record. The site itself is fully visible on the public internet.

steps.title: CT feed alerts the SOC
steps.caption: The intelligence stream matches the new certificate against brand keywords and raises an alert. The SOC reviews it as likely staging, days before any mail is sent.
steps.defender: This is the earliest useful moment. The alert alone is weak, but domain age plus a brand keyword is a strong pair.

steps.title: Phishing mail reaches a user
steps.caption: The attacker sends mail that links to the fresh site. A user clicks. The mail gateway sees a valid TLS link on a domain with no history and low reputation.
steps.defender: The mail gateway logs the domain. One weak signal appears; on its own it rarely blocks a message.

steps.title: Credentials typed over valid TLS
steps.caption: The user opens the page. The browser shows the padlock because the certificate is valid, and the user submits the login form. The proxy records a POST to a days-old domain.
steps.defender: Proxy and DNS logs hold the full picture: young domain, fresh certificate, form POST. This matches the CT alert from step 4.

detection.detail: A weak signal exists but is not yet a confirmed alert.

steps.title: Stolen credentials get tested
steps.caption: The attacker collects the credentials and logs in as the user from an unfamiliar country and device. Identity systems flag impossible travel.
steps.defender: Identity telemetry sees a login that does not fit the user pattern. This is often the first high-confidence signal of the case.

fields.detail: The attacker collects the credentials and logs in as the user from an unfamiliar country and device.

detection.label: Alert raised
detection.detail: The SOC has enough evidence to open an incident.

steps.title: The SOC closes the loop
steps.caption: The SOC joins the CT alert, the proxy record, and the identity alert. The team blocks the domain, resets the user credentials, and saves a permanent CT watch rule for the brand.
steps.defender: Minutes of certificate visibility became a full case. Blocking at the domain stage stops the campaign before any host is infected.
